title: The Little Book of Common Sense Investing

accepted_claims.text: The conclusion reiterates regular saving, broad exposure, cost control and disciplined adherence while explicitly acknowledging uncertainty about future stock and bond returns.

adversarial_review: Repeated maxims and endorsements are not additional independent trials. The aggregate arithmetic cannot guarantee positive wealth growth, prove every discretionary strategy inferior, or justify unconditional investing despite urgent liabilities. The acknowledgments identify Vanguard-supported research and separate the author's opinions from current management's views.

consolidated_memory.text: Bogle frames a broad, low-cost, enduring market holding as a way to retain market returns while accepting market losses; his guarantee concerns relative participation, not positive absolute returns.
The book uses historical returns and assumed future business growth to motivate compounding; those examples do not establish a forward return promise.
In the closed-family parable, changing ownership among investors cannot increase their aggregate claim on business proceeds; intermediary fees and extra taxes reduce what the family retains.
Bogle derives a general preference for minimal intermediation from the aggregate cost argument, rather than establishing that every individual adviser or active strategy is worthless.
Bogle decomposes stock returns into dividend yield, earnings growth and a valuation-multiple component, distinguishing business results from changing investor expectations.
He treats long-run business fundamentals as more dependable than short-run sentiment forecasts, while warning that historical returns containing valuation expansion are poor extrapolations.
Capitalization weighting keeps portfolio weights aligned with changing relative prices without requiring a rebalance solely because those prices move.
The book explicitly calls its S&P 500 versus total-market return comparison period dependent and recommends comparing active funds with indexes matching their strategies.
The chapter expands investment costs beyond expense ratios to sales charges, turnover, spreads, market impact and cash drag.
The fifty-year example contrasts assumed 7% and 5% annual returns to demonstrate compounding cost drag; it is hypothetical rather than a forecast or a literal accounting of intermediary revenue.
Bogle presents recurring expenses and turnover costs as more persistent fund-selection inputs than recent performance rankings.
Exhibit 5.1 compares cost quartiles over 1991–2016 but explicitly includes only surviving funds; its reported advantage and risk-adjusted results therefore require that selection caveat.
The chapter distinguishes price appreciation from total return with dividends reinvested and shows that omission of distributions can substantially distort a long-horizon comparison.
It documents several large historical dividend cuts despite describing dividends as comparatively stable, so dividend income cannot be treated as guaranteed.
Time-weighted fund returns and dollar-weighted investor experience answer different questions because the latter includes the timing and size of contributions and withdrawals.
Bogle attributes an additional investor return shortfall to timing and selection, while acknowledging that the precise estimated gap is uncertain.
The chapter's turnover-related tax argument concerns taxable holdings and explicitly sets aside investors holding solely in tax-deferred accounts.
Lower fees can leave more distributable dividend income and therefore more dividend tax even when the investor retains more income after tax.
Bogle labels his forward return estimate an informed guess and varies dividend, growth and terminal valuation assumptions; the figures are 2017 scenarios rather than current forecasts.
The chapter illustrates that a correct aggregate return forecast can result from offsetting errors in its investment-return and valuation components.
The high historical association between initial bond yields and subsequent returns is useful evidence but does not make a bond fund's quoted yield an unconditional guaranteed holding-period return.
The chapter follows the starting population of funds, including closures, and shows that identifying surviving winners retrospectively differs from selecting them in advance.
The Magellan and Contrafund case histories suggest that manager changes and asset growth can alter the conditions behind an earlier record.
The book reports weak persistence in fund return rankings across consecutive five-year periods, with merged and closed funds retained as a separate outcome.

Regression toward average observed performance cautions against treating an extreme recent rank as persistent skill, but does not establish that all skill is absent or supply a contrarian trading rule.
Bogle distinguishes an adviser's possible planning, allocation and behavioral benefits from the separate claim of selecting market-beating funds.
The chapter acknowledges that its negative fund-selection evidence is dated or anecdotal and that intangible advisory benefits remain possible.
Index products tracking substantially the same portfolio can deliver different net results because their expenses and sales charges differ.
The chapter's simulated active-fund success probabilities depend on declared cost and return-process assumptions; they are not universal empirical odds for every investment rule.
Bonds may support allocation discipline and reduce portfolio volatility even when their expected long-run return is lower than stocks; the risk reduction is conditional on the exposures held.
A higher bond-fund yield can reflect longer maturity or weaker credit rather than manager skill, so comparisons need matched maturity and credit quality.
Despite criticizing ETF speculation, Bogle explicitly permits long-term ownership of broad-market indexed ETFs.
A product's trading convenience and narrow exposure can encourage costly timing and concentration; these behavioral concerns must be distinguished from the wrapper's own portfolio costs.
Rule-based factor weighting still makes an active exposure choice relative to a capitalization-weighted market, even if implementation is called passive.
The chapter warns that selecting factor products using attractive historical results can embed data mining, while its own small set of comparisons cannot settle every factor strategy's future value.
Bogle presents Graham's distinction between a demanding businesslike active process and a diversified defensive approach suited to investors without that capacity.
The historical Graham interview and Buffett anecdote are evidence reported by Bogle, rather than independent reading of Graham's full work or a new source in this Character's curriculum.
The chapter separates financial ability to bear risk from willingness to experience it, tying allocation to liabilities, available assets and time rather than a universal stock percentage.
Fixed-allocation rebalancing is presented as a risk-control choice distinct from discretionary tactical timing; neither has a guaranteed return benefit.
Bogle calls age-based allocation a flexible starting heuristic and asks investors to inspect target-date funds' underlying holdings and costs.
He favors US-only equity exposure but acknowledges that past relative outperformance may have changed valuations and leaves future international relative returns uncertain.
The chapter supports a total-return withdrawal approach while explicitly declining to guarantee a fixed withdrawal rule's sustainability.
The conclusion reiterates regular saving, broad exposure, cost control and disciplined adherence while explicitly acknowledging uncertainty about future stock and bond returns.

memory_delta: Retain the foundation as a falsifiable default, not a slogan. The book is read; profitable performance, current legal accuracy and prospective superiority remain unestablished.

rejected_claims.text: The claim that diversification leaves only market risk is too broad for an operational system: implementation, liquidity, liabilities and behavioral failures remain relevant.

accepted_claims.text: Capitalization weighting keeps portfolio weights aligned with changing relative prices without requiring a rebalance solely because those prices move.

adversarial_review: An aggregate gross-return identity is not identical to an equal-weighted fund ranking. Index composition changes still create turnover. Historical SPIVA results are reported by the source and have not been independently reproduced here.

adversarial_review: A capitalized benefit stream is neither liquid nor interchangeable with tradable bonds. The Social Security example extending deferral to age 72, arbitrary valuation discount, retirement-account descriptions and contribution figures need primary-source verification before practical use. The withdrawal wording needs an explicit initial-capital versus current-balance convention. Historical US versus EAFE performance is period dependent and EAFE is not every non-US market.

benchmark: S&P 500 total return in USD, with distributions reinvested. Freeze on 2026-09-30 the public eligible population of US-domiciled unleveraged open-end S&P 500 index mutual funds. One cheapest non-advisory share class purchasable for USD 10000 without another account per distinct underlying portfolio; break fee ties by ascending public fund identifier. Rank by stated annual expense ratio plus applicable entry/exit charges for that holding period, retain all closures and mergers, and split into quartiles with ties assigned by the same identifier. Require at least 20 distinct portfolios and five unrelated management organizations overall, otherwise inconclusive. Use equal initial capital and no later contributions. Missing terminal proceeds make the comparison inconclusive; never drop a failure.
failure_condition: Lowest-cost minus highest-cost mean net total return is less than or equal to zero. Unavailable permissions, incomplete data, population below minimum, or mismatched exposure yield inconclusive/not-run, never a passing result.
horizon: One prospective year; proposed research only. If inputs and approvals are not ready before the start, expire this registration and append a new one before any later window.
prediction: The mean net total return of the lowest prospective all-in-cost quartile exceeds that of the highest-cost quartile among the frozen eligible portfolios; no result has been observed.

assumptions: Fund mandates, fee schedules and investor eligibility are observable before evaluation begins.
Returns include reinvested distributions and all applicable entry, exit and recurring costs.
Securities lending, sampling, cash balances and operational differences may affect tracking independently of fees.
invalidation_conditions: The lower-cost group does not achieve the predicted positive net-return difference over the registered window.
Exposure matching, fee eligibility, complete population coverage or independent fund count cannot be established; mark the test inconclusive rather than a success.
minimal_logic_chain: Match index exposure and total-return conventions before comparing funds.
Recurring expenses subtract from the proceeds available to the investor.
Lower expenses should leave a smaller net tracking shortfall if other implementation differences do not offset them.
position: Among comparable funds tracking the same broad equity index, lower recurring costs should predict a smaller net return shortfall over a predeclared period.
predicted_observables: The lower-cost quartile has a higher equal-weighted mean net total return, and hence a smaller shortfall to the same S&P 500 total-return benchmark, than the higher-cost quartile.
rebuttals: Retain closures and mergers, compare only matched mandates, and count distinct portfolios rather than share classes.
Report the preregistered difference and implementation caveats even when they challenge the foundational prior.
scope: Proposed prospective study of US-domiciled, USD, unleveraged open-end mutual funds tracking the S&P 500; no current investment recommendation or executed experiment.
strongest_counterarguments: Tracking implementation and lending revenue can dominate a small fee difference over one year.
Share classes are correlated and a winner-survivor sample can create a spurious result.
One prospective year cannot establish universal or permanent superiority.
